catalog_quote: § 28. The question of stress in Ila presents considerable difficulty. As has been observed in the previous paragraph, in emphasis and repetition for clearness, the phenomenon of two adjacent stressed syllables in one word has been noticed. Apart from this, however, the main stress in Ila normally falls on the penultimate syllable. When this is the case I have left the stress unmarked; but there are numerous cases of ultimate main stress, e.g. ijt (egg) majt (eggs) v6sé (all of them). With many words, especially trisyllabic words, a raised tone on the first syllable gives an impression of stress. The first syllable, however, is not stressed, e.g. mahuta (fat). Again, in many cases, the tone on the final syllable of the word is either raised or kept at the same pitch as the preceding syllable; this, with a certain "snappiness" of enunciation, gives the impression of stress on the final …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Doke 1928 section 28 passage, the section 27 secondary-stress passage, the 'one and only one main stress' line and orthography item (ix) are all present verbatim (the scanned textbreaks aside) in the held Bantu Studies vol. 3 text at the stated pages; Smith 1907 secondary quotes also confirmed. (2) Deciding source is a 1928 phonetic outline by C. M. Doke -- old, but written by a phonetician who explicitly separates stress from tone, and it is the most explicit stress statement that exists for Ila: Glottolog lists no later grammar/phonology, and the web/repository search (TUFS-ILCAA, UNZA DSpace, archive.org, Bickmore bibliography) found only tone-only modern work. (3) Newly downloaded Smith & Dale 1920 p. 281 independently confirms 'stress, if any, usually falls on the penultimate' (with enclitic-driven final stress and stem-vowel secondary stress), so the fixed and weight-blind pen

sources.citation: Yukawa, Yasutoshi. 1987. イラ語動詞アクセント試論 / A tentative tonal analysis of Ila verbs. Journal of Asian and African Studies (ILCAA, Tokyo) 33: 127-180. Open PDF:https://tufs.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/1793/files/jaas033007.pdf(image-only, Japanese; postscript p. 180 says the English translation appears as 'A Tonological Study of Ila Verbs' in Studies in Zambian Languages, Bantu Linguistics (ILCAA) vol. 1, 1987).
sources.quote: No stress statement anywhere read: 'accent' (アクセント) is transcribed purely as pitch -- acute = high vowel, circumflex = high-to-low fall, unmarked = low ('in conventional writing accent is not marked', p. 128); verbs split into a 'peaked' type (kúpa, kúbuzha, kútanda: H on prefix) vs. a peakless type, analysed morpheme-by-morpheme as H/L. Notably the nouns í-yî 'egg', má-yî 'eggs' (p. 128, classes III/XII) -- Doke's own examples of 'ultimate main stress' ('ije', 'maje') -- carry a final falling (HL) tone, suggesting Doke's final-stress exceptions are tonal percepts rather than a second stress p
sources.locator: pp. 127-129 (transcription conventions, noun-class list, infinitive tone types), p. 167 (conclusion); pages read as rendered images
sources.note: The only modern prosodic study of Ila (fieldwork 1984-85, Namwala district); tone-only analysis, silent on stress, but shows Doke's 'ultimate stress' items egg/eggs as final HL tone -- should be cited in tone_note and in the exceptions caution.

sources.quote: '( : lengthens the preceding vowel ; ' indicates stress falling on the next syllable.) The tone in Ila is often very important as distinguishing words of different meaning ... The stress, if any, usually falls on the penultimate, but in long words there is also a secondary stress on the stem-vowel ; compare the word utu'leke'le.'le given above, where the stem is lek-. Monosyllables are largely treated as enclitics and draw the stress forward to the final syllable ; for example : amb'i:la, speak to ; uambila:'nɛ ? Why do you speak ? The stress often marks difference of meaning ; for example, 'a
sources.locator: p. 281 (the scanned text), after the IPA Lord's Prayer specimen
sources.note: Independent pre-Doke statement 'The stress, if any, usually falls on the penultimate' plus secondary stress on the stem vowel and enclitic-driven final stress (p. 281); worth adding as a confirming citation to a record that currently rests on Doke 1928 alone.

sources.quote: 'The findings show that both Tonga and Ila use tone and length for grammatical and lexical purposes' ... 'Tonga and Ila realises two basic tones namely, high (H) and low (L)' with minimal pairs (ma՛la 'nails' vs mala 'small intestines'); vowel length contrastive. Stress/accent placement is never mentioned.
sources.locator: section 5.7 'Suprasegmental variation in Tonga and Ila', pp. 61-63
sources.note: Recent native-region description of Ila suprasegmentals (tone + length only, no stress); documents that current descriptions do not posit word stress, relevant to the record's tone caveat.
